reasoning: Set A fits the ground truth much more closely and teaches RL more soundly. Its tank is circular. Fish are scored on how long they survive. There is a single learning predator. Each environment has a ladder of concepts: table-based learning, then DQN, then the full-grid CNN, with ablations for memory, target copy and exploration. The fish tank goes from REINFORCE to PPO, then a school, then limited vision. Predator-prey goes from fixed opponents to naive co-learning to self-play against an opponent pool, with cross-play. Each claim is tested against the baselines and a library reference. Its M1 is one coherent slice that ends with a demonstration: the real 5-seed ladder beats both baselines, matches the library, and can be replayed. Set B is clean and well organised, with smaller pipelines, a useful method-check gate and write-ups, and it gives strong oracles for its statistics tasks. But it departs from the brief: the tank is square, fish are scored by hits per fish (lower is better), and there are 2 predators. It also spends its first two milestones on Snake, and M2 is a leftover bundle (replay viewer, video, reference check, the real DQN's memory and target network, and the 'beats baselines' verdict). So M1's exit never shows that an agent learns or that you can watch it. Its DQN spine is plain online Q-learning, and the step it calls 'PPO' is REINFORCE. A has its own problems. Some 'revised core' wording is stale. The brief says future environments aren't being designed, yet the spec designs them. Snake.reset_to returns an array while core.Env is keyed by team. PL-01 is overloaded with constructor rows. Small helpers (gae, returns_to_go) are frozen into the contract. Some packets leave out types they need. Overall, A's plan is the more faithful and more instructive one.

strengths: Faithful to the brief: circular tank, survival score, one learning predator, prey foraging for pellets
Clear concept ladders (tabular→DQN→CNN; REINFORCE→PPO→school→limited vision; fixed→co-learning→pool self-play) plus ablations
Precise closed-form golden cases for the Snake rules and the compact view, with exact expected observations
M1 exit requires real 5-seed runs that beat both baselines and match the library within the time limits
Stable-Baselines3 parameter mapping and the 'one learner, others frozen' adapter are well thought through
weaknesses: Stale framing about revising the core and replanning is left in the spec, roadmap and architecture risks
PL-01 lists 16 rows, including environment constructors and agent classes that aren't steps in call order
Frozen helper functions (returns_to_go, gae, clipped_objective) in the contract
The M1-T06 spine packet leaves out the core.Transition shape and runs.create_run, which it needs
Long and dense for a solo learner

strengths: Small, readable pipelines, each with a clear entry function and real minimal spine versions
The method-check gate (a two-exit corridor whose answer is worked out by hand) is a good guard against silent RL bugs
Strong statistics oracles (permutation test, Holm correction, verdict rule)
Write-ups and a finish check support the goal of 'explain why it works'
Clear dependency graph whose fakes let the spines run in parallel
weaknesses: Square tank, a hits-per-fish score and 2 predators depart from the ground truth
S1 split into M1 and a leftover M2 (replay, video, reference check, the real DQN, beats-baselines verdict); M1 never shows an agent learning or a replay
No value-learning vs policy-gradient ladder within an environment; the 'PPO' spine is REINFORCE under PPO's name
Leftover open questions in pipelines.md were already resolved by AD-10
Snake observation encoding is never pinned down, so the oracles are only properties

A: M1-T06: the packet leaves out the core.Transition definition (which the loop must build), runs.create_run (to get a RunWriter), core.TeamSpec/SOLO, and evaluate.ScoreSet/GameRecording (needed for the 5 recorded games)
M1-T01: one task freezes every type, fake and fixture across 11 components; the Size M label understates it
